topicTitle: Transcendental Equations in a Complex Variable

questions.prompt: Why does \(e^z=0\) have no complex solution?
questions.answer: Write \(z=x+iy\). Then \(|e^z|=e^x\), and \(e^x>0\) for all real \(x\), so \(e^z\) can never be zero.
Write \(1=e^{2\pi ik i}\). Matching modulus gives \(\operatorname{Re}(z)=0\), and matching argument gives \(\operatorname{Im}(z)=2\pi k\). Thus \(z=2\pi ik\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Write \(-1=e^{i(\pi+2\pi k)}\). Therefore \(z=i(\pi+2\pi k)=(2k+1)\pi i\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
The target has modulus \(e^3\) and argument \(0\) modulo \(2\pi\). Hence \(z=3+2\pi ik\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Write \(i=e^{i(\pi/2+2\pi k)}\). Thus \(z=i(\pi/2+2\pi k)\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Write \(1+i=\sqrt2e^{i(\pi/4+2\pi k)}\). Matching modulus gives \(\operatorname{Re}(z)=\ln\sqrt2=\tfrac12\ln2\), so \(z=\tfrac12\ln2+i(\pi/4+2\pi k)\).
Use the solution of \(e^w=1\): \(2z=2\pi ik\). Therefore \(z=\pi ik\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Set \(z+1=i(\pi+2\pi k)\). Then \(z=-1+i(\pi+2\pi k)\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Use \(\sinh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/2\). Setting this to zero gives \(e^z=e^{-z}\), so \(e^{2z}=1\). Hence \(2z=2\pi ik\), and \(z=\pi ik\).
Using \(\cos z=(e^{iz}+e^{-iz})/2\), multiply by \(2e^{iz}\) to get \(e^{2iz}+1=0\). Thus \(e^{2iz}=-1=e^{i(\pi+2\pi k)}\), so \(z=\pi/2+\pi k\).
\(\sin z=(e^{iz}-e^{-iz})/(2i)=0\) gives \(e^{iz}=e^{-iz}\). Multiplying by \(e^{iz}\), \(e^{2iz}=1\), so \(2iz=2\pi ik\), hence \(z=\pi k\).
Substitute: \(e^{2\pi ik}=\cos(2\pi k)+i\sin(2\pi k)=1+0i=1\). Therefore every integer \(k\) gives a solution.
Write \(8=e^{\ln8+2\pi ik i}\). Then \(3z=\\ln8+2\pi ik\), so \(z=\ln2+\frac{2\pi i k}{3}\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Allow all arguments of the target: \(2e^{i(\pi/3+2\pi k)}\). Thus \(z=\ln2+i(\pi/3+2\pi k)\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).

questions.prompt: For which integers \(k\) does \(z=\pi ik\) solve both \(e^{2z}=1\) and \(e^z=1\)?
questions.answer: All \(z=\pi ik\) solve \(e^{2z}=1\). For \(e^z=1\), we need \(\pi k\) to be a multiple of \(2\pi\), so \(k\) must be even.
This means \(e^z\) is real. Write \(z=x+iy\); then \(e^z=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)\). We need \(\sin y=0\), so \(y=\pi k\), and \(z=x+i\pi k\) with \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
\(\cosh z=(e^z+e^{-z})/2=0\). Multiplying by \(2e^z\) gives \(e^{2z}+1=0\), so \(e^{2z}=-1=e^{i(\pi+2\pi k)}\). Hence \(z=i(\pi/2+\pi k)\), with \(k\in\mathbb Z\).

questions.prompt: A learner solves \(e^z=1\) and gives only \(z=0\). Explain the error.
questions.answer: The learner found one solution but ignored periodicity in the imaginary direction. Since \(e^{z+2\pi i}=e^z\), every \(z=2\pi ik\) with \(k\in\mathbb Z\) solves the equation.

questions.prompt: Explain why the fundamental theorem of algebra gives no count for the solutions of \(e^z=1\).
questions.answer: The fundamental theorem of algebra applies only to polynomial equations. The equation \(e^z=1\) is transcendental and has infinitely many solutions \(z=2\pi ik\), so polynomial root-counting does not apply.

questions.prompt: Show that \(e^{az}=1\), with non-zero complex \(a\), has infinitely many solutions and give them.
questions.answer: The equation \(e^w=1\) has solutions \(w=2\pi ik\). Put \(w=az\); since \(a\ne0\), divide by \(a\) to get \(z=2\pi ik/a\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\). Distinct integers give an infinite periodic solution set along a complex line.
